## NCOMMS-24-44820-T Response to Reviewers

## Reviewer 1

1. 'The dynamic range seems to be relatively limited and may limit the impact of this technology. I wonder if the authors have performed some optimisations such as increasing the stoichiometry of the deubiquitination domain or combine different deubiquitination domains.'
2. 'I would also recommend to consider methodologies to enhance dynamic range.'

We thank the reviewer for this point. For optimization of our duAb architecture, we demonstrate across several protein targets that we can achieve potent levels of stabilization via our OTUB1 catalytic domain when compared to other potent DUBs, as determined by Poirson et al . Specifically, we only maintain the C-terminal catalytic domain of human OTUB1, and we swap out the N-terminal natural substrate-binding domain with the various target-protein domains that we test in our subsequent experiments. In our previous work, we attempted to enhance this domain by replacing lysine residues to prevent autoubiquitination of our duAb architecture, but we did not observe any differences in target stabilization and thus did not warrant incorporation into this study. However, we'd like to point the reviewer to Figure 3, where we design a genetically-encodable, deliverable platform via lipid nanoparticles (LNPs). As highlighted in Figures 3C and 3D, we found that we could achieve significant levels of p53 stabilization and increased apoptosis activation with just 1 μg p53\_pMLM\_4-OTUB1. Thus our dynamic range was sufficient to induce functional downstream consequences.

2. 'Figure 2D and 2E present non stabilising fusions. It would be helpful to understand what may be the reason.'

We thank the reviewer for addressing this. As we now highlight in our discussion, we write about the key differences in the UCHL1 and UBC9 domains that result in the inefficiency of these fusions. Specifically, UBC9 has been shown to regulate stabilization of various targets via SUMOylation, which does not involve the direct deubiquitination of different substrates. Furthermore, while UCHL1 was shown to be an effective DUB for monoubiquitinated proteins, its active site structure prevents the catalytic domain from binding to polyubiquitinated proteins, which we hypothesize lends to its 'non-stabilizing' effect in our fusion architecture.

3. 'I was wondering why OTUB1 is used in the systems instead of the others listed OTUD1, UCHL1, or UBC9. Is the selection based on one target generalizable?'

We thank the reviewer for this point. Expanding upon our initial experiments on evaluating different, potent DUB domains (Figures 1B-1C), we additionally tested the same four DUB catalytic domain candidates linked to our experimentally-validated, computationally-derived SaLT&PepPr peptide βcat\_SnP\_7 (Figure 1D), which we demonstrate that the OTUB1 catalytic domain still exhibited the most stabilization of β-catenin-sfGFP levels. We also tested an additional SaLT&PepPr-derived peptide - βcat\_SnP\_8 - and exhibited significantly more stabilization of β-catenin-sfGFP when comparing the OTUB1 fusion with the second best candidate OTUD1 (Supplementary Figure 2). Furthermore, when comparing all four functional domains in our Wnt signaling functional assay (as described in Figure 1G), we show that β-catenin-sfGFP stabilization yielded the most effective increase in Wnt signaling for our OTUB1 fusion when comparing the other domains (Figure 1H and Supplementary Figure 3).

4. 'As a side note, I do not share the comparison with CRISPR. CRISPR is a DNA or RNA programmable system which uses sequence identity. It is RNA-programmed and this work uses peptides, and CRISPR is programmed by sequence identity whereas this work uses generative AI. I do not see the analogy.' 'As a more general comment, I strongly believe that the discussion should be extended and discuss more the results. Now it is mostly centered on comparison to CRISPR or interesting future perspectives.'

'I would recommend to revise the discussion and complement the data in figure 2.'

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion and viewpoint. We have omitted the CRISPR analogy to our modular duAb architecture, and have now included a thorough discussion and analysis of our results. We hypothesize the reasoning for our observed results when selecting our stabilizing DUB domain, and we highlight the modularity of using our platform for different classes of protein binders. Furthermore, we extend our discussion to describe future work and perspectives for the use and impact of our technology.

## Reviewer 2:

1. 'The authors cite the preprint version of this work, while it was already published in April 2024 and the citation should be updated.'

We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have updated our citations to include the already published article.

2. 'What is noteworthy is that the published version of the manuscript has some additional experiments in comparison to the cited preprint version which puts in question whether OTUB1-mediated stabilization is caused by deubiquitination or rather inhibition of the E2 enzymes and ubiquitination. The results presented in Fig. 1C and Fig. 2B show that the use of the pan-DUB inhibitor only partially reduces the effect of duAb. Using duAbs with catalytically inactive OTUB1 (C91 mutation) and a mutant with additional mutations inhibiting E2 binding (D88/H265) would help to further deconvolute the postulated mechanism of action of duAbs. Adding a supplementary figure with these mutant versions of duAbs and their effect on the stabilization of the chosen substrate would provide direct evidence on whether duAbs work by active substrate deubiquitination.'

We thank the reviewer for this noteworthy suggestion. In Figure 1, we expanded upon our experiments for duAb mechanistic validation by including two OTUB1 mutants: one where we just mutate the catalytic C91 (OTUB1 C91S) and another where we mutate all residues of OTUB1's catalytic triad D88A, C91S, and H265A (OTUB1 ASA). Performing these experiments by linking these mutants to both the YFP Nb and our computationally-derived peptide βcat\_SnP\_7, we demonstrate that these mutations impeded KCNQ1-YFP and β-catenin-sfGFP stabilization.

3. 'Additional comments regarding figures:
- a. I suggest the authors to align horizontally the X axes of the graphs in Fig. 1B and 1C and adjust the graphs so that they have equal dimensions. I also recommend adjusting the origin of the Y axis on Fig. 1C so that it starts at 0.
- b. I suggest the authors to align vertically the Y axes of the graphs in Fig. 1C and 1E.
- c. The title on the Y axis in Fig. 1E is the same as on Fig. 1C. It should be changed to the Wnt signaling activation presented in the graph.
- d. I recommend changing the Y axis on Fig. 1E to a discontinuous axis. This will allow to keep the resolution of the changes while also showing the extent of the Wnt signaling activation more accurately as in the current scale, at first glance the 10% difference appear as 2-fold increase.
- e. In Fig. 2C the technical replicates are represented as equivalent to biological repeats which should be avoided as it could reduce the P-value and influence the statistics of the experiment. I suggest the authors do not treat these equally and only use the biological repeats for plotting and statistical analysis (as recommended in the Nature Communications data guidelines).'

We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. We have carefully reviewed our figures and made the suggested edits regarding the x-axis alignments for Figures 1B and 1C, y-axis alignments and titles in Figures 1C and 1E, and the discontinuous axis and altered scale for Figure 1E. In addition, we omitted our two additional technical replicates from our statistical analysis and plots in Figure 2C, ensuring only biological replicates were used for analysis.

4. 'Other minor concerns regarding the manuscript are a few inconsistencies between the figure legends and the Materials and Methods section:
- a. The authors describe using pcDNA3 vector for duAbs expression in Materials and Methods and in Fig. 1, but in a legend of Fig. 2 they mention using pCMV which was not listed elsewhere. The pCMV constructs should be therefore added to the Materials and Methods section.
- b. In Fig. 2D the authors use HeLa cells, which should be added to Materials and Methods.'

We appreciate the reviewer for noticing these inconsistencies in the text and figures. We only used pcDNA3 vectors, so we made this correction for the Figure 2 legend. We have also added HeLa cells to our Materials and Methods section under the 'Cell culture' section.

## Reviewer 3:

'Hong and Chatterjee report the design of 'deubiquibodies' (duAbs) for YFP, ß-catenin as well as p53, WEE1 and FOXO1 to induce deubiquitination and stabilization of the POI. The deubiquibodies are based on short, computationally-designed peptide guides fused to the catalytic domain of OTUB1, a potent deubiquitinase. While the presented data is consistent unfortunately, I feel the data lacks the significance warranted for publication in a high value journal such as Nature Communications. Thus, I cannot support publication in Nature Communications.

The strategy of protein stabilization via deubiquitination has already been known for quite a while since the report of DUBTACs in 2022. Furthermore, the stabilization of YFP via enDUBO1 has also been known since 2020. While improving the efficacy of the system and showing its broad applicability, using the also predeveloped guide peptides, is great work from which the community will greatly benefit, I don't consider it enough for Nature Communications. Additionally, CRISPR is mentioned as a neat way to introduce the duAbs, the presented work was not done via CRISPR modification. However, my main concern is the lack of any PD effects or readouts besides protein levels. All modifications have not been conducted in a disease relevant cell line or context and no downstream effect of the POI stabilization has been shown. Simply showing protein stabilization is in my opinion not enough to warrant publication in Nature Communications. Therefore, I recommend transferring the manuscript to ACS Chemical Biology or RSC Chemical Biology instead.'

We thank the reviewer for this feedback and appreciate the opportunity to argue for our paper's publication in Nature Communications . While we reference both DUBTAC and enDUBO1 studies, we believe that we build upon and add our own novelty. First, we identify by comparing multiple deubiquitinase domains (OTUD1, which is in the enDUBO1 architecture, UCHL1, UBC9, and OTUB1). We optimize upon the original enDUBO1

architecture by comparing multiple deubiquitinase domains (shown in Figure 1B, 1D, Supplementary Figure 2) and report a more significant increase in KCNQ1-YFP expression when repeating their experimental layout.

Additionally, we expand upon the novelty of this stabilizing architecture by replacing a known YFP nanobody with protein language model-derived peptides, which introduces highly programmable TPS , which has not been previously achieved. We demonstrate consistently that we can perform plug-and-play of these peptides into our duAb architecture, and now target therapeutically-relevant targets that were previously intractable (no small molecule warhead or off-the-shelf antibody/nanobody).

Specifically, we extend this application to several other key, disease-driving target proteins, namely FOXP3, a transcription factor regulating T regulatory cell function, WEE1, a tumor suppressor kinase downregulated in several cancers, and PAX3::FOXO1, a fusion oncoprotein driver of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, a completely disordered, undruggable target. Most notably, we designed potent p53-targeting duAbs using a purely target-conditioned language model. To take it even further, we encoded these duAbs as mRNA, delivered them via clinically-relevant lipid nanoparticles, and not only exhibited significant stabilization but also apoptosis activation via hallmark cleaved PARP-1 expression.

Overall, this paper provides the unique ability for anyone to stabilize a desired protein target of interest. All they have to do is just run an algorithm, clone generated sequences into plasmid vectors, transfect them into cells, and read out protein levels. In our opinion, it's just as easy as CRISPR, but just for proteins rather than DNA. The fact that these can also be encoded as mRNA and delivered via LNPs further makes a strong translational argument for our technology as well.

In total, we hope that the reviewer will reconsider their position and suggest publication in Nature Communications ! Thank you!

## NCOMMS-24-44820A Response to Reviewers

## Reviewer 2:

1. 'The manuscript is improved in comparison to the first submitted version. The Authors included the suggested controls and added data for OTUB1 inactive mutants. The Authors also included new experiments on LNP delivery of duAbs and downstream effects induced by targeted protein stabilization, which supports the potential applicability of the presented approach. However, I still consider duAbs as an easily customizable research tool for studying protein stabilization and target validation rather than a potential therapeutic approach. The manuscript does not address several issues which would help to determine the potential scope of the presented method. '

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. While we envision our duAbs can be extended into biotherapeutics space, we now emphasize the immediate utility of duAbs for studying protein stabilization. In particular, we focus on the applicability of applying our duAbs to proteins of interest that are currently considered undruggable or uncharacterized by conventional small molecule-based approaches, namely those that are structurally disordered or lack suitable binding pockets.

2. 'Figure 3 C and D show that LNP delivery of 2 ug of duAb has lower potency than 1 ug dose. The Authors should comment on the possible explanation in the Discussion section of the manuscript. '

We thank the reviewer for this feedback. In the Discussion, we now hypothesize that we observe lower potency of 2 μg of duAb delivery due to the hook effect. A previous study by Patel et al. (PMID: 37515040) showed that increasing the overall mRNA payload did not directly correlate with delivery efficiency. As a result, increasing the dosage of duAb-expressing mRNA may have yielded less p53-targeting duAb expression and less observed p53 stabilization.

3. 'A time-course experiment would give an insight into the level of protein stabilization that can be achieved using duAbs and how quickly they act.'
2. We thank the reviewer for this point. We have now performed a time-course experiment for our β-catenin-targeting duAbs, βcat\_SnP\_7 and βcat\_SnP\_8, two SaLT&PepPr-derived peptides that exhibit nanomolar binding affinity to β-catenin. As shown in Figure 2D , we demonstrate that while we observe significant increases of β-catenin-sfGFP expression starting at the 24 hour time point for our βcat\_SnP\_7-OTUB1 fusion, we observed the most consistent stabilization for both β-catenin-targeting duAbs after 48 hours. Additionally, we see that this stabilizing effect plateaued between 48-72 hours, showing that we can achieve maximal, potent duAb activity within 72 hours post-transfection.
4. 'I would recommend the Authors include comparative proteomics data for a chosen duAb and polyG-OTUB1 to address the selectivity of duAbs and potential off-target effects which could arise from increasing cellular levels of OTUB1 catalytic domain.'

We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. Expanding on our duAb characterization in Figure 2, we have now conducted a comparative proteomics experiment comparing our non-targeting polyG-OTUB1 to our β-catenin-targeting duAb using βcat\_SnP\_7. As shown in Figure 2H , we demonstrate that we selectively increase both exogenous β-catenin-sfGFP and endogenous β-catenin in HEK293T cells while yielding minimal off-target effects (also shown by directly comparing protein abundances between our polyG and βcat\_SnP\_7 samples in Figures 2I and 2J ). Upon further analysis of the other upregulated proteins, we observed that these changes in protein expression are likely due to downstream regulation as a result of β-catenin stabilization. Most notably, Axin 2 is another regulator of Wnt signaling, so we expect this to increase as we stabilize β-catenin (which is also corroborated by our other β-catenin stabilization data in the rest of Figure 2). Additionally, we interestingly notice that NEIL1, a DNA glycosylase that has been shown to initiate colorectal cancer phenotypes by destabilizing DNA damage, is upregulated. In total, however, there are very few off-targets, suggesting that our duAbs are quite specific to the target of interest.

## Reviewer 3:

1. 'Thanks a lot for the revised manuscript and the rebuttal letter. While I like the manuscript in general, I still don't see it fit for Nature Communications. The concept is not novel and has been around for a few years.'

We thank the reviewer for their feedback and appreciate the opportunity to clarify the novelty and impact of our work. While we clearly acknowledge prior work in targeted protein stabilization, including DUBTACs and enDUBO1, our approach substantially builds upon and advances these concepts in multiple ways. First, we systematically compare multiple deubiquitinase domains (OTUD1, UCHL1, UBC9, and OTUB1) to optimize stabilization efficiency, demonstrating that OTUB1 significantly outperforms other candidates -- this was not done in previous works. Second, we introduce a modular, programmable architecture by replacing traditional small-molecule warheads or known nanobody-based binders with peptides generated from protein language models. This enables a highly versatile stabilization platform applicable to undruggable targets, including transcription factors and disordered oncoproteins. Importantly, we validate this approach on several clinically relevant targets-including β-catenin, FOXP3, WEE1, and PAX3::FOXO1-showing that duAbs achieve stabilization in a highly specific and tunable manner. Finally, we take this further by demonstrating that duAbs can be encoded as mRNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), significantly broadening their translational potential. These innovations collectively establish our work as more than a reiteration of existing stabilization strategies; rather, it represents a new, programmable paradigm for intracellular protein modulation. We humbly urge the reviewer to reconsider their viewpoint in light of our data.

2. 'Furthermore, while claiming everything can work with CRISPR no CRISPR has been used in the manuscript.'

While we understand the reviewer's concerns about our initial mention of CRISPR (and this was removed in the previous revision of the manuscript), we did not claim that our system uses CRISPR; rather, we drew an analogy to illustrate the accessibility and ease of use of our duAb platform. Just as CRISPR allows for programmable genome editing via a simple guide RNA, our duAbs enable programmable protein stabilization by swapping in short, computationally-designed peptides. This comparison was meant to highlight the generalizability and plug-and-play nature of our system, which allows users to stabilize virtually any protein of interest by simply running an algorithm, cloning a sequence, and transfecting cells. Again, we removed this in the previous iteration, so a mention of CRISPR will not be made in the final version.

3. 'No work has been done in actual disease relevant cell lines and no downstream signaling has been evaluated. Everything is done based in protein levels.'

While we thank the reviewer for their comment, we must point out that this is factually incorrect. Our manuscript clearly demonstrates stabilization in multiple disease-relevant models, including hepatocellular carcinoma cells for WEE1 stabilization, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma cells  for

PAX3::FOXO1 stabilization, and cervical carcinoma cells for p53 stabilization. Furthermore, we assess functional consequences beyond just protein abundance, particularly in our p53 experiments, where we show apoptosis activation via cleaved PARP-1 expression following duAb treatment. We also show Wnt signaling changes via the TOP-GFP assay for our β-catenin experiments. Overall, our data directly establish that our duAbs not only stabilize proteins but also induce meaningful downstream effects, addressing the reviewer's concern.

Given these points, we respectfully disagree with the reviewer's assertion that our work lacks novelty or biological relevance. Our study presents the first computationally-driven, modular, and genetically encodable protein stabilization platform, capable of targeting previously intractable proteins with therapeutic potential. We hope that these clarifications will allow the reviewer to reconsider their stance and recognize the significant contributions of our work. Thank you for your thoughtful review.

This is an important piece of research since there are very few works describing tools for TPS and the field would benefit greatly from more accessible and adaptable TPS tools. While the duAb described in the manuscript have limited direct therapeutic potential, they can be a valuable method for validating targets for putative development of small molecule stabilisers.
